headline: Ni is from Middle Chinese 二 (nyijH, “two”).
Tobu is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, from Proto-Japonic *tənpu.
Hen is from Middle Chinese 變 (MC pjenH).
Naru is possibly a verbalization of na-, the bound form of 音 (ne, “sound”).
Oyogu was possibly oyoku, but Ryūkyūan cognates support a voiced g at the end.
Yasumi is the stem form of the verb 休む (yasumu, “to rest”).
Fueru is from the Classical Japanese verb 増ゆ (fuyu).
Itasu is the transitive/causative counterpart to the intransitive verb 至る (itaru).
Uru is Old Japanese, and possibly cognate with 得る (eru, “to obtain”), from getting money for the item sold.
Itai was itasi in Old Japanese, and might originally have been an interjection like English ouch.
Iro was first attested in the Nihon Shoki meaning “color”, with the romance senses appearing from the 900s.
Niku is from Middle Chinese 肉 (MC nyuwk).
Kikoeru is from 聞こゆ (kikoyu), built on kika, the irrealis of 聞く (kiku, “to hear”), plus ゆ (-yu).
Hajimaru is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pansimara, “to begin”, intransitive.
Oriru is from the classical upper bigrade verb 降る (oru).
Ikiru is from the classical upper bigrade verb 生く.
Fuku “clothes” is from Middle Chinese 服 (MC bjuwk).
Ōkina is the na-adjective form of 大きい, appearing from the Muromachi period.
Hashi is tentatively traced to Proto-Japonic *pasui, and probably related to 挟む (hasamu, “to pinch”).
Me is probably cognate with 見る (miru, “to see”), and may also be cognate with 芽 (me, “bud, shoot”).
Dare was tare until around the Edo period, voiced by analogy with 何れ (dore) and 何処 (doko).
Owari is the stem form of the verb 終わる (owaru, “to end”).
Daijōbu is from Chinese 大丈夫, equivalent to 大 (dai-) plus 丈夫 (jōbu).
Yūmei is likely from Middle Chinese 有名, literally “to have + name”.
Tsukamaeru is possibly 掴ま (tsukama, “to grab”) plus ふ (fu, frequentative suffix).
Mimi is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, from Proto-Japonic *mimi.
Dōbutsuen is 動物 (dōbutsu, “animal”) plus 園 (-en, “garden”).
Kimaru is the intransitive form of the Old Japanese verb 決む (kimu, “to decide”).
Kawaku is cognate with 渇く (kawaku, “to be thirsty”).
